title: Gerrymandering: How to Stifle Democracy
summary: Josh and Chuck explain gerrymandering: how the House of Representatives is apportioned after each census, how vague redistricting rules let dominant state parties draw skewed maps, the origin of the term in 1812 with Governor Elbridge Gerry and the "salamander" map, cracking and packing techniques, the efficiency gap metric, prison gerrymandering, nonpartisan commissions (Canada and several US states), and Supreme Court reluctance to intervene (Gill v. Whitford, Texas and other cases). The episode closes with a listener mail about bone marrow registry donation.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with dad jokes and banter about Jim Gaffigan, then introduce the topic of gerrymandering as a newsy PSA-style episode.

segments.title: How the House of Representatives is apportioned
segments.summary: The hosts explain the House's design: two-year terms, seats tied to population, the 435-seat cap set in 1912, and the Reapportionment Act requiring redistribution after each census. They note the vague rules for drawing district boundaries that let dominant parties draw maps.

segments.title: Break and transition to history
segments.summary: Brief mid-episode break before the hosts turn to historical examples.

segments.title: Early history and the origin of the term gerrymander
segments.summary: Early examples include Patrick Henry redrawing Virginia's fifth district to pit James Madison against James Monroe. The term comes from Governor Elbridge Gerry of Massachusetts, whose 1812 map was compared by the Boston Gazette to a salamander. Early Congress attempted rules but they were hard to enforce, and the Dakota territories were split into two states to gain Senate and electoral votes.

segments.title: Modern gerrymandering, partisan consultants and polarization
segments.summary: Modern map-drawing uses sophisticated software and block-level census data, with consultants simulating future elections. Wisconsin's Assembly map is cited as an example. The hosts argue polarization has worsened the problem and that the Brennan Center found most gerrymandered districts sit in seven swing states.

segments.title: Break and transition to techniques
segments.summary: A short break before the hosts describe the main techniques.

segments.title: Cracking, packing, and the efficiency gap
segments.summary: Cracking dilutes opposing voters across districts; packing concentrates them into few districts. The hosts explain wasted votes and the efficiency gap metric devised by Nicholas Stephanopoulos, with a suggested seven percent threshold.

segments.title: Prison gerrymandering
segments.summary: Some states count prisoners toward district population even though they cannot vote, giving more weight to voters in districts with prisons, such as a ward in Iowa; a few states have ruled this unconstitutional.

segments.title: Nonpartisan commissions and Supreme Court involvement
segments.summary: The hosts argue only nonpartisan commissions can fix the problem, citing Canada's 1960s commission and commissions in California, Arizona, Washington, Idaho, New Jersey and Hawaii. They discuss Gill v. Whitford being sent back on standing grounds and the Supreme Court's reluctance to rule on maps, including Texas and the Voting Rights Act, with remarks by Gorsuch and Thomas.

segments.title: Listener mail: bone marrow registry
segments.summary: A listener named Chris shares that his father died of AML after a bone marrow treatment and asks listeners to register with Be The Match Bone Marrow Registry.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to share ideas and contact the show via social media, website, or email.
